Reference: De Groote and Verboven (2019)

Model Setting

Households make a dynamic decision on whether and when to adopt residential solar photovoltaic (PV) systems. In each period ttt, a household iii can either not adopt, j=0j=0j=0, or adopt one of JJJ PV systems with different capacity sizes, j=1,…,Jj=1,\ldots,Jj=1,…,J. Adoption is a terminating action: once a household installs a PV system, it exits the adoption problem, while non-adoption preserves the option to adopt in a future period.

Household iii chooses the alternative that maximizes:

Uijt=vijt+ϵijt,(8.1.1.1)U_{ijt}=v_{ijt}+\epsilon_{ijt}, \tag{8.1.1.1}Uijt​=vijt​+ϵijt​,(8.1.1.1)

where ϵijt\epsilon_{ijt}ϵijt​ follows an i.i.d. Type-I extreme value distribution. In the baseline aggregate model, households are homogeneous apart from these idiosyncratic taste shocks.

For an adoption alternative j=1,…,Jj=1,\ldots,Jj=1,…,J, the conditional value is:

vijt=δjt=xjtγ−αpjt(β)+ξjt,(8.1.1.2)v_{ijt}=\delta_{jt}=x_{jt}\gamma-\alpha p_{jt}(\beta)+\xi_{jt}, \tag{8.1.1.2}vijt​=δjt​=xjt​γ−αpjt​(β)+ξjt​,(8.1.1.2)

where xjtx_{jt}xjt​ contains alternative-specific characteristics, α\alphaα measures price sensitivity, ξjt\xi_{jt}ξjt​ is an unobserved demand shock, and pjt(β)p_{jt}(\beta)pjt​(β) is the net lifetime cost of adopting PV system jjj.

The net price combines the upfront investment cost and the discounted stream of future benefits:

pjt(β)=pjtINV(β)−ρtG(β)pjtGCC−ρE(β)pjtEL,(8.1.1.3)p_{jt}(\beta) = p^{INV}_{jt}(\beta) - \rho_t^G(\beta)p^{GCC}_{jt} - \rho^E(\beta)p^{EL}_{jt}, \tag{8.1.1.3}pjt​(β)=pjtINV​(β)−ρtG​(β)pjtGCC​−ρE(β)pjtEL​,(8.1.1.3)

where pjtGCCp^{GCC}_{jt}pjtGCC​ denotes future Green Current Certificate subsidies and pjtELp^{EL}_{jt}pjtEL​ denotes electricity bill savings from net metering. The capitalization factors are:

ρtG(β)=1−(βG)RtG1−βG,ρE(β)=1−(βE)RE1−βE,(8.1.1.4)\rho_t^G(\beta) = \frac{1-(\beta^G)^{R_t^G}}{1-\beta^G}, \qquad \rho^E(\beta) = \frac{1-(\beta^E)^{R^E}}{1-\beta^E}, \tag{8.1.1.4}ρtG​(β)=1−βG1−(βG)RtG​​,ρE(β)=1−βE1−(βE)RE​,(8.1.1.4)

with:

βG=(1−λ)(1−π)β,βE=(1−λ)(1+ϑ)β,(8.1.1.5)\beta^G=(1-\lambda)(1-\pi)\beta, \qquad \beta^E=(1-\lambda)(1+\vartheta)\beta, \tag{8.1.1.5}βG=(1−λ)(1−π)β,βE=(1−λ)(1+ϑ)β,(8.1.1.5)

where λ\lambdaλ captures physical depreciation, π\piπ is inflation, and ϑ\varthetaϑ is the growth rate of real electricity prices.

The upfront investment cost also incorporates future tax credits:

pjtINV(β)=pjtGROSS−∑τ=14β12τtaxcutjtτ.(8.1.1.6)p^{INV}_{jt}(\beta) = p^{GROSS}_{jt} - \sum_{\tau=1}^{4}\beta^{12\tau}taxcut^{\tau}_{jt}. \tag{8.1.1.6}pjtINV​(β)=pjtGROSS​−τ=1∑4​β12τtaxcutjtτ​.(8.1.1.6)

The discount factor β\betaβ therefore determines how households value future financial benefits relative to current installation costs.

Dynamic Adoption Decision

If the household does not adopt in period ttt, it receives the current utility of waiting plus the discounted option value of future adoption:

δ0t=u0t+βEtVˉt+1,(8.1.1.7)\delta_{0t} = u_{0t} + \beta E_t\bar{V}_{t+1}, \tag{8.1.1.7}δ0t​=u0t​+βEt​Vˉt+1​,(8.1.1.7)

where Vˉt+1\bar{V}_{t+1}Vˉt+1​ is the ex ante continuation value. Under the Type-I extreme value assumption:

Vˉt+1=0.577+ln⁡(∑j=0Jexp⁡(δj,t+1)).(8.1.1.8)\bar{V}_{t+1} = 0.577+ \ln\left( \sum_{j=0}^{J}\exp(\delta_{j,t+1}) \right). \tag{8.1.1.8}Vˉt+1​=0.577+ln(j=0∑J​exp(δj,t+1​)).(8.1.1.8)

Rather than specifying a stochastic transition process for future prices and subsidies, the authors write:

ηt=Vˉt+1−EtVˉt+1,(8.1.1.9)\eta_t = \bar{V}_{t+1} - E_t\bar{V}_{t+1}, \tag{8.1.1.9}ηt​=Vˉt+1​−Et​Vˉt+1​,(8.1.1.9)

where ηt\eta_tηt​ is a mean-zero expectation error. Hence:

δ0t=u0t+β(Vˉt+1−ηt).(8.1.1.10)\delta_{0t} = u_{0t} + \beta(\bar{V}_{t+1}-\eta_t). \tag{8.1.1.10}δ0t​=u0t​+β(Vˉt+1​−ηt​).(8.1.1.10)

Using the Hotz–Miller conditional choice probability inversion and taking j=1j=1j=1 as a reference terminating alternative:

Vˉt+1=0.577+δ1,t+1−ln⁡S1,t+1.(8.1.1.11)\bar{V}_{t+1} = 0.577 + \delta_{1,t+1} - \ln S_{1,t+1}. \tag{8.1.1.11}Vˉt+1​=0.577+δ1,t+1​−lnS1,t+1​.(8.1.1.11)

After normalizing u0t+0.577β=0u_{0t}+0.577\beta=0u0t​+0.577β=0, the value of waiting becomes:

δ0t=β(δ1,t+1−ln⁡S1,t+1−ηt).(8.1.1.12)\delta_{0t} = \beta \left( \delta_{1,t+1} - \ln S_{1,t+1} - \eta_t \right). \tag{8.1.1.12}δ0t​=β(δ1,t+1​−lnS1,t+1​−ηt​).(8.1.1.12)

Choice Probabilities and Market Share Inversion

The Type-I extreme value assumption implies logit choice probabilities:

Sjt=exp⁡(δjt)∑j′=0Jexp⁡(δj′t).(8.1.1.13)S_{jt} = \frac{\exp(\delta_{jt})} {\sum_{j'=0}^{J}\exp(\delta_{j't})}. \tag{8.1.1.13}Sjt​=∑j′=0J​exp(δj′t​)exp(δjt​)​.(8.1.1.13)

The adoption share of alternative jjj is defined as:

Sjt=qjtNt,(8.1.1.14)S_{jt} = \frac{q_{jt}}{N_t}, \tag{8.1.1.14}Sjt​=Nt​qjt​​,(8.1.1.14)

where qjtq_{jt}qjt​ is the number of new adopters and:

Nt=N−∑τ<t∑j=1Jqjτ(8.1.1.15)N_t = N- \sum_{\tau<t}\sum_{j=1}^{J}q_{j\tau} \tag{8.1.1.15}Nt​=N−τ<t∑​j=1∑J​qjτ​(8.1.1.15)

is the remaining population of potential adopters. The non-adoption share is:

S0t=1−∑j=1JSjt.(8.1.1.16)S_{0t} = 1-\sum_{j=1}^{J}S_{jt}. \tag{8.1.1.16}S0t​=1−j=1∑J​Sjt​.(8.1.1.16)

Using the Berry market share inversion:

ln⁡(SjtS0t)=δjt−δ0t.(8.1.1.17)\ln\left(\frac{S_{jt}}{S_{0t}}\right) = \delta_{jt}-\delta_{0t}. \tag{8.1.1.17}ln(S0t​Sjt​​)=δjt​−δ0t​.(8.1.1.17)

Estimating Equation

Combining the dynamic value of waiting with the market share inversion gives the main estimating equation:

ln⁡(SjtS0t)=(xjt−βx1,t+1)γ−α[pjt(β)−βp1,t+1(β)]+βln⁡S1,t+1+ejt,(8.1.1.18)\ln\left(\frac{S_{jt}}{S_{0t}}\right) = (x_{jt}-\beta x_{1,t+1})\gamma - \alpha \left[ p_{jt}(\beta) - \beta p_{1,t+1}(\beta) \right] + \beta\ln S_{1,t+1} + e_{jt}, \tag{8.1.1.18}ln(S0t​Sjt​​)=(xjt​−βx1,t+1​)γ−α[pjt​(β)−βp1,t+1​(β)]+βlnS1,t+1​+ejt​,(8.1.1.18)

where:

ejt=ξjt−β(ξ1,t+1−ηt).(8.1.1.19)e_{jt} = \xi_{jt} - \beta \left( \xi_{1,t+1}-\eta_t \right). \tag{8.1.1.19}ejt​=ξjt​−β(ξ1,t+1​−ηt​).(8.1.1.19)

The equation relates current adoption to current and future investment opportunities. For forward-looking households, adoption today is less attractive when future PV prices are expected to fall, while a pre-announced reduction in future subsidies increases adoption before the policy change.

If β\betaβ were known and all explanatory variables were exogenous, the equation could be estimated linearly. In practice, β\betaβ is unknown and enters both directly and nonlinearly through pjt(β)p_{jt}(\beta)pjt​(β), so the model is estimated using nonlinear GMM.

Identification and GMM Estimation

The model is estimated using the moment conditions:

E[zjtejt]=0,(8.1.1.20)E[z_{jt}e_{jt}]=0, \tag{8.1.1.20}E[zjt​ejt​]=0,(8.1.1.20)

where zjtz_{jt}zjt​ is a vector of instruments.

The upfront investment price may be endogenous because installers can charge higher prices when demand is high. To identify the price sensitivity α\alphaα, the authors use the price index of Chinese PV modules in the European market as a cost shifter. Module prices are strongly related to installation costs but are assumed not to respond directly to local PV demand shocks.

The discount factor β\betaβ is identified primarily from variation in the future GCC benefits. The GCC subsidy schedule varies substantially over time and across capacity choices, while the upfront investment cost enters current utility separately. This variation identifies how households trade off current investment costs against future financial benefits.

A second source of identification comes from pre-announced changes in GCC subsidies. A future reduction in subsidies does not affect the payoff from adopting before the reform, but lowers the value of waiting and adopting afterward. The resulting increase in adoption immediately before subsidy reductions therefore contains information about the discounting of future adoption opportunities.

For a candidate parameter vector:

θ=(α,β,γ),(8.1.1.21)\theta=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma), \tag{8.1.1.21}θ=(α,β,γ),(8.1.1.21)

the model implies residuals ejt(θ)e_{jt}(\theta)ejt​(θ) and sample moments:

g(θ)=1JT∑j,tzjtejt(θ).(8.1.1.22)g(\theta) = \frac{1}{JT} \sum_{j,t} z_{jt}e_{jt}(\theta). \tag{8.1.1.22}g(θ)=JT1​j,t∑​zjt​ejt​(θ).(8.1.1.22)

The GMM estimator chooses:

θ^=arg⁡min⁡θg(θ)′Wg(θ).(8.1.1.23)\hat{\theta} = \arg\min_{\theta} g(\theta)'Wg(\theta). \tag{8.1.1.23}θ^=argθmin​g(θ)′Wg(θ).(8.1.1.23)

The authors first use the excluded instruments together with the exogenous product characteristics, and then use an approximation to optimal instruments to improve efficiency. The estimated monthly discount factor can be converted into an annual implicit interest rate as:

r=β−12−1.(8.1.1.24)r=\beta^{-12}-1. \tag{8.1.1.24}r=β−12−1.(8.1.1.24)

Local Market Heterogeneity

The baseline model is extended to allow for persistent household heterogeneity across MMM local markets. For households in market mmm, the conditional value of adopting alternative jjj becomes:

vmjt=xjtγ−αpjt+ξjt+wjtλm,(8.1.1.25)v_{mjt} = x_{jt}\gamma - \alpha p_{jt} + \xi_{jt} + w_{jt}\lambda_m, \tag{8.1.1.25}vmjt​=xjt​γ−αpjt​+ξjt​+wjt​λm​,(8.1.1.25)

where:

λm=ΛDm,(8.1.1.26)\lambda_m=\Lambda D_m, \tag{8.1.1.26}λm​=ΛDm​,(8.1.1.26)

and DmD_mDm​ contains local demographic characteristics such as income, household size, house size, and local-market fixed effects. The interactions allow price sensitivity and preferences for PV capacity to vary systematically across markets.

Because adoption shares are frequently zero at the highly disaggregated local-market level, the authors do not directly apply the Berry share inversion within each market. Instead, they combine the aggregate GMM moments with micro-moments derived from the local-market likelihood. These moments match demographic-product correlations and total local adoption rates between the data and the model. The next-period local choice probability entering the dynamic model is estimated in a first stage.

  • De Groote, Olivier and Frank Verboven. 2019. “Subsidies and time discounting in new technology adoption: Evidence from solar photovoltaic systems.” American Economic Review, 109(6): 2137–2172.

This is the random-utility representation of the household's discrete choice in month ttt. The index iii is a household that has not yet adopted, j=0j=0j=0 is waiting and j=1,…,Jj=1,\ldots,Jj=1,…,J are PV systems of different capacity. The term vijtv_{ijt}vijt​ is the conditional value of alternative jjj: it is not a one-period flow utility but the full expected present value of choosing jjj today, including everything that follows from that choice. For an adoption alternative it is the lifetime net benefit of the system, given in equation (2); for j=0j=0j=0 it contains the option value of adopting later, given in equation (7). The term ϵijt\epsilon_{ijt}ϵijt​ is an idiosyncratic taste shock, independent across households, alternatives and months, with the Type-I extreme value distribution function

F(ϵ)=exp⁡(−e−ϵ).F(\epsilon)=\exp\left(-e^{-\epsilon}\right).F(ϵ)=exp(−e−ϵ).

The additive, i.i.d. extreme value form buys three closed forms used later: the expected maximum in equation (8), the logit choice probabilities in equation (13), and the one-to-one map between continuation values and choice probabilities in equation (11). What it rules out is persistent unobserved heterogeneity: since vijtv_{ijt}vijt​ does not vary with iii in the baseline, the households that remain in the market are a random sample of the population, so there is no dynamic selection among the remaining non-adopters. The scale of utility is fixed by the unit variance parameter of ϵijt\epsilon_{ijt}ϵijt​, which is why the price coefficient α\alphaα in equation (2) is identified.

For j=1,…,Jj=1,\ldots,Jj=1,…,J the conditional value is common to all households and is written as a mean utility δjt\delta_{jt}δjt​. The row vector xjtx_{jt}xjt​ collects observed characteristics of system jjj in month ttt (a constant, capacity-size dummies and similar controls) with coefficients γ\gammaγ. The variable pjt(β)p_{jt}(\beta)pjt​(β) is the net present cost of the system in real money units, built up in equations (3) to (6); it depends on the discount factor β\betaβ because future subsidies and savings are capitalized. The coefficient α>0\alpha>0α>0 is the marginal utility of money, so −αpjt(β)-\alpha p_{jt}(\beta)−αpjt​(β) converts the net cost into utils. The term ξjt\xi_{jt}ξjt​ is a demand shock for system jjj in month ttt that households observe and the econometrician does not; it becomes part of the error in equation (19).

Because adoption is a terminating action, δjt\delta_{jt}δjt​ has no continuation term: all future flows from the system are already inside pjt(β)p_{jt}(\beta)pjt​(β). A single α\alphaα multiplies the whole net price, so a unit of upfront cost and a unit of properly discounted future benefit have the same utility weight. That restriction is what lets the response to future benefits, relative to the response to upfront costs, reveal β\betaβ. The implied semi-elasticity of the odds of adopting jjj relative to waiting is, by equation (17) and holding δ0t\delta_{0t}δ0t​ fixed,

∂ln⁡(Sjt/S0t)∂pjt=−α.\frac{\partial \ln\left(S_{jt}/S_{0t}\right)}{\partial p_{jt}}=-\alpha .∂pjt​∂ln(Sjt​/S0t​)​=−α.

The net price is the upfront cost minus the present value of the two benefit streams. Let s=0,1,2,…s=0,1,2,\ldotss=0,1,2,… count months since adoption, and let bjt,sGb^{G}_{jt,s}bjt,sG​ and bjt,sEb^{E}_{jt,s}bjt,sE​ be the real GCC payment and the real electricity saving received sss months after adopting system jjj in month ttt. ρ≈1−0.0610.0116≈81,\rho\approx\frac{1-0.061}{0.0116}\approx 81,ρ≈0.01161−0.061​≈81,

These are the per-month factors by which the present value of each benefit flow shrinks. Start with the GCC stream. A system produces certificates in proportion to its electricity output, and output falls at the monthly physical depreciation rate λ\lambdaλ, so output sss months after adoption is (1−λ)s(1-\lambda)^{s}(1−λ)s times initial output. The certificate price is guaranteed in nominal terms, so with monthly inflation π\piπ its real value after sss months is (1+π)−s≈(1−π)s(1+\pi)^{-s}\approx(1-\pi)^{s}(1+π)−s≈(1−π)s times the initial one. Discounting by βs\beta^{s}βs, the present value of the real GCC payment at horizon sss is

βs(1−λ)s(1−π)s pjtGCC=[(1−λ)(1−π)β]spjtGCC=(βG)s pjtGCC.\beta^{s}(1-\lambda)^{s}(1-\pi)^{s}\,p^{GCC}_{jt}=\left[(1-\lambda)(1-\pi)\beta\right]^{s}p^{GCC}_{jt}=(\beta^{G})^{s}\,p^{GCC}_{jt}.βs(1−λ)s(1−π)spjtGCC​=[(1−λ)(1−π)β]spjtGCC​=(βG)spjtGCC​.

For electricity savings the quantity saved again falls with (1−λ)s(1-\lambda)^{s}(1−λ)s, while the real electricity price grows at monthly rate ϑ\varthetaϑ, so

βs(1−λ)s(1+ϑ)s pjtEL=[(1−λ)(1+ϑ)β]spjtEL=(βE)s pjtEL.\beta^{s}(1-\lambda)^{s}(1+\vartheta)^{s}\,p^{EL}_{jt}=\left[(1-\lambda)(1+\vartheta)\beta\right]^{s}p^{EL}_{jt}=(\beta^{E})^{s}\,p^{EL}_{jt}.βs(1−λ)s(1+ϑ)spjtEL​=[(1−λ)(1+ϑ)β]spjtEL​=(βE)spjtEL​.

Reading off the terms in square brackets,

βG=(1−λ)(1−π)β,βE=(1−λ)(1+ϑ)β.\beta^G=(1-\lambda)(1-\pi)\beta, \qquad \beta^E=(1-\lambda)(1+\vartheta)\beta .βG=(1−λ)(1−π)β,βE=(1−λ)(1+ϑ)β.

Two remarks. First, (1−π)(1-\pi)(1−π) is a first-order approximation to the exact real deflator 1/(1+π)1/(1+\pi)1/(1+π); the difference is of order π2\pi^{2}π2 per month and negligible at monthly rates. Second, λ\lambdaλ, π\piπ and ϑ\varthetaϑ must be expressed per month to be consistent with the monthly β\betaβ; they are calibrated outside the model, so β\betaβ is the only unknown in βG\beta^GβG and βE\beta^EβE. Since βG<β\beta^G<\betaβG<β, a fixed nominal subsidy is discounted more heavily than β\betaβ alone suggests, while βE\beta^EβE can exceed β\betaβ if electricity prices rise faster than panels degrade.

This defines the upfront component of the net price. The term pjtGROSSp^{GROSS}_{jt}pjtGROSS​ is the gross installation price of system jjj in month ttt, paid at adoption and therefore not discounted. The variable taxcutjtτtaxcut^{\tau}_{jt}taxcutjtτ​ is the income tax reduction that an adopter in month ttt receives τ\tauτ years later; the investment tax credit could be spread over up to four tax years, hence τ=1,…,4\tau=1,\ldots,4τ=1,…,4. Because β\betaβ is a monthly discount factor, a benefit arriving τ\tauτ years ahead is discounted by β12τ\beta^{12\tau}β12τ. The tax credits are known amounts fixed by the rules in force at the adoption date, so they are treated as part of the investment cost rather than as a flow like the GCC subsidies.

The equation makes pjtINVp^{INV}_{jt}pjtINV​ a function of β\betaβ, which is one of the reasons the estimating equation (18) is nonlinear in β\betaβ. It also shows a first place where the discount factor matters: a more patient household values the delayed tax credit more. For example, with a single credit taxcutjt1taxcut^{1}_{jt}taxcutjt1​ and β=0.9884\beta=0.9884β=0.9884,

pjtINV=pjtGROSS−0.988412 taxcutjt1≈pjtGROSS−0.87 taxcutjt1,p^{INV}_{jt}=p^{GROSS}_{jt}-0.9884^{12}\,taxcut^{1}_{jt}\approx p^{GROSS}_{jt}-0.87\,taxcut^{1}_{jt},pjtINV​=pjtGROSS​−0.988412taxcutjt1​≈pjtGROSS​−0.87taxcutjt1​,

so a credit paid one year later is worth 87 percent of its face value. The result feeds into equation (3). The gross price is the component treated as endogenous in estimation, see equation (20).

This is the conditional value of not adopting, the counterpart of equation (2) for j=0j=0j=0. A household that waits gets the flow utility u0tu_{0t}u0t​ of living without a PV system this month and remains in the market, so next month it again faces the full choice set. Its continuation payoff is the expected value of behaving optimally from t+1t+1t+1 on, before next month's taste shocks are drawn:

Vˉt+1=Eϵ[max⁡j=0,…,J(δj,t+1+ϵij,t+1)].\bar{V}_{t+1}=E_{\epsilon}\left[\max_{j=0,\ldots,J}\left(\delta_{j,t+1}+\epsilon_{ij,t+1}\right)\right].Vˉt+1​=Eϵ​[j=0,…,Jmax​(δj,t+1​+ϵij,t+1​)].

The operator EtE_tEt​ is the expectation over the aggregate state of month t+1t+1t+1 (prices, subsidy rules, demand shocks) given what households know in month ttt, and β\betaβ is the same monthly discount factor that capitalizes future benefits in equations (3) to (6). This is the Bellman equation of an optimal stopping problem written in terms of alternative-specific values: adoption stops the problem with payoff δjt\delta_{jt}δjt​, waiting continues it with payoff δ0t\delta_{0t}δ0t​.

The term βEtVˉt+1\beta E_t\bar{V}_{t+1}βEt​Vˉt+1​ is the option value of waiting. It rises when future systems are expected to be cheaper or better and falls when a subsidy cut is announced, which is how the model produces adoption spikes before announced cuts. If β=0\beta=0β=0 in this term the model collapses to a static logit with outside good utility u0tu_{0t}u0t​. Equations (8) to (12) turn the unobserved expectation into observables.

The ex ante value is the expected maximum over alternatives in month t+1t+1t+1, where each ϵij,t+1\epsilon_{ij,t+1}ϵij,t+1​ has distribution function F(ϵ)=exp⁡(−e−ϵ)F(\epsilon)=\exp(-e^{-\epsilon})F(ϵ)=exp(−e−ϵ). Write δj\delta_jδj​ for δj,t+1\delta_{j,t+1}δj,t+1​ and ϵj\epsilon_jϵj​ for ϵij,t+1\epsilon_{ij,t+1}ϵij,t+1​. By independence, the distribution function of the maximum is the product of the individual ones:

Pr⁡(max⁡j(δj+ϵj)≤y)=∏j=0JPr⁡(ϵj≤y−δj)=∏j=0Jexp⁡(−e−(y−δj))=exp⁡(−e−y∑j=0Jeδj).\begin{aligned} \Pr\left(\max_{j}\left(\delta_{j}+\epsilon_{j}\right)\le y\right) &=\prod_{j=0}^{J}\Pr\left(\epsilon_{j}\le y-\delta_{j}\right) =\prod_{j=0}^{J}\exp\left(-e^{-(y-\delta_{j})}\right)\\ &=\exp\left(-e^{-y}\sum_{j=0}^{J}e^{\delta_{j}}\right). \end{aligned}Pr(jmax​(δj​+ϵj​)≤y)​=j=0∏J​Pr(ϵj​≤y−δj​)=j=0∏J​exp(−e−(y−δj​))=exp(−e−yj=0∑J​eδj​).​

Define the inclusive value I=ln⁡∑j=0JeδjI=\ln\sum_{j=0}^{J}e^{\delta_{j}}I=ln∑j=0J​eδj​, so that ∑jeδj=eI\sum_{j}e^{\delta_{j}}=e^{I}∑j​eδj​=eI. Then

Pr⁡(max⁡j(δj+ϵj)≤y)=exp⁡(−e−(y−I)),\Pr\left(\max_{j}\left(\delta_{j}+\epsilon_{j}\right)\le y\right)=\exp\left(-e^{-(y-I)}\right),Pr(jmax​(δj​+ϵj​)≤y)=exp(−e−(y−I)),

which is again a Type-I extreme value distribution, shifted to location III. The mean of a standard Type-I extreme value variable is Euler's constant,

∫−∞∞ϵ e−ϵexp⁡(−e−ϵ)dϵ=0.5772…,\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\epsilon\,e^{-\epsilon}\exp\left(-e^{-\epsilon}\right)d\epsilon=0.5772\ldots,∫−∞∞​ϵe−ϵexp(−e−ϵ)dϵ=0.5772…,

so the mean of the maximum is the location plus this constant:

Vˉt+1=E[max⁡j(δj,t+1+ϵij,t+1)]=0.577+ln⁡(∑j=0Jexp⁡(δj,t+1)).\bar{V}_{t+1}=E\left[\max_{j}\left(\delta_{j,t+1}+\epsilon_{ij,t+1}\right)\right]=0.577+\ln\left(\sum_{j=0}^{J}\exp(\delta_{j,t+1})\right).Vˉt+1​=E[jmax​(δj,t+1​+ϵij,t+1​)]=0.577+ln(j=0∑J​exp(δj,t+1​)).

The sum includes j=0j=0j=0, so Vˉt+1\bar{V}_{t+1}Vˉt+1​ depends on δ0,t+1\delta_{0,t+1}δ0,t+1​ and hence, recursively, on all later periods. Equation (11) removes this recursion.

This equation defines the expectation error ηt\eta_tηt​ as the difference between the continuation value that is actually realized in month t+1t+1t+1 and what households expected it to be in month ttt. It is a definition, but it carries the behavioral assumption of the paper: households have rational expectations, so their forecast is the true conditional mean. Taking EtE_tEt​ of both sides gives

Etηt=EtVˉt+1−EtVˉt+1=0,E_t\eta_t=E_t\bar{V}_{t+1}-E_t\bar{V}_{t+1}=0,Et​ηt​=Et​Vˉt+1​−Et​Vˉt+1​=0,

and by the law of iterated expectations ηt\eta_tηt​ is uncorrelated with any variable ztz_tzt​ in the month-ttt information set:

E[ztηt]=E[ztEtηt]=0.E\left[z_t\eta_t\right]=E\left[z_tE_t\eta_t\right]=0.E[zt​ηt​]=E[zt​Et​ηt​]=0.

The sign convention is that ηt>0\eta_t>0ηt​>0 when the future turns out better than expected, for example when prices fall by more than forecast.

What this buys is that the researcher never has to specify or estimate the stochastic process that governs prices, subsidies and demand shocks, nor solve the dynamic program. The unobserved expectation is replaced by its realization minus an error, as in Euler-equation estimation, and the error is moved into the residual of equation (19). What it costs is that ηt\eta_tηt​ is correlated with every variable dated t+1t+1t+1, so those variables must be instrumented with month-ttt information, see equation (20). The assumption does not require perfect foresight; perfect foresight is the special case ηt=0\eta_t=0ηt​=0. Note that ηt\eta_tηt​ is common to all alternatives in month ttt, so averaging it out relies on a long time dimension.

Start from the value of waiting in equation (7),

δ0t=u0t+βEtVˉt+1.\delta_{0t}=u_{0t}+\beta E_t\bar{V}_{t+1}.δ0t​=u0t​+βEt​Vˉt+1​.

Rearranging the definition of the expectation error in equation (9) gives the expected value in terms of the realized one:

EtVˉt+1=Vˉt+1−ηt.E_t\bar{V}_{t+1}=\bar{V}_{t+1}-\eta_t.Et​Vˉt+1​=Vˉt+1​−ηt​.

Substituting,

δ0t=u0t+β(Vˉt+1−ηt).\delta_{0t}=u_{0t}+\beta\left(\bar{V}_{t+1}-\eta_t\right).δ0t​=u0t​+β(Vˉt+1​−ηt​).

Nothing has been assumed beyond equation (9). The step matters because Vˉt+1\bar{V}_{t+1}Vˉt+1​, unlike its expectation, can be expressed through next month's observed market shares, which is done in equation (11).

The goal is to express the log-sum in equation (8) through one observable choice probability. Write the logit probability of equation (13) one month ahead for the adoption alternative j=1j=1j=1:

Take logs and solve for the log of the denominator:

ln⁡S1,t+1=δ1,t+1−ln⁡(∑j=0Jexp⁡(δj,t+1))⟹ln⁡(∑j=0Jexp⁡(δj,t+1))=δ1,t+1−ln⁡S1,t+1.\ln S_{1,t+1}=\delta_{1,t+1}-\ln\left(\sum_{j=0}^{J}\exp(\delta_{j,t+1})\right) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \ln\left(\sum_{j=0}^{J}\exp(\delta_{j,t+1})\right)=\delta_{1,t+1}-\ln S_{1,t+1}.lnS1,t+1​=δ1,t+1​−ln(j=0∑J​exp(δj,t+1​))⟹ln(j=0∑J​exp(δj,t+1​))=δ1,t+1​−lnS1,t+1​.

The interpretation is that the expected value of the whole choice problem equals the value of one particular alternative plus a correction −ln⁡S1,t+1≥0-\ln S_{1,t+1}\ge 0−lnS1,t+1​≥0, which is large when that alternative is rarely chosen, that is when the other options (including waiting) are comparatively attractive. The identity holds for any reference alternative, but only a terminating one is useful: δ1,t+1\delta_{1,t+1}δ1,t+1​ is given by equation (2) and contains no further continuation value, whereas choosing j=0j=0j=0 as the reference would bring back δ0,t+1\delta_{0,t+1}δ0,t+1​ and the recursion. The choice j=1j=1j=1 is otherwise arbitrary.

Substitute the inversion in equation (11) into the value of waiting in equation (10):

δ0t=u0t+β(0.577+δ1,t+1−ln⁡S1,t+1−ηt)=(u0t+0.577β)+β(δ1,t+1−ln⁡S1,t+1−ηt).\begin{aligned} \delta_{0t}&=u_{0t}+\beta\left(0.577+\delta_{1,t+1}-\ln S_{1,t+1}-\eta_t\right)\\ &=\left(u_{0t}+0.577\beta\right)+\beta\left(\delta_{1,t+1}-\ln S_{1,t+1}-\eta_t\right). \end{aligned}δ0t​​=u0t​+β(0.577+δ1,t+1​−lnS1,t+1​−ηt​)=(u0t​+0.577β)+β(δ1,t+1​−lnS1,t+1​−ηt​).​

The first bracket contains only the flow utility of waiting and a constant. Imposing the normalization u0t+0.577β=0u_{0t}+0.577\beta=0u0t​+0.577β=0 leaves

δ0t=β(δ1,t+1−ln⁡S1,t+1−ηt).\delta_{0t}=\beta\left(\delta_{1,t+1}-\ln S_{1,t+1}-\eta_t\right).δ0t​=β(δ1,t+1​−lnS1,t+1​−ηt​).

The normalization is not innocuous in the way a static outside-good normalization is: in a dynamic discrete choice model the flow utility of one alternative has to be fixed in every state for identification, and here it is fixed to a constant that does not vary over time. The value of waiting is now a function of one future mean utility, one future market share, the discount factor and an expectation error. No value function has to be computed and no beliefs about periods beyond t+1t+1t+1 have to be specified, because whatever happens after t+1t+1t+1 is summarized by the share S1,t+1S_{1,t+1}S1,t+1​.

This holds for j=0j=0j=0 as well, with δ0t\delta_{0t}δ0t​ the value of waiting from equation (12). Because the remaining households are homogeneous up to ϵijt\epsilon_{ijt}ϵijt​, the individual choice probability equals the share of remaining households choosing jjj, which is what links the model to the data in equation (14).

This is the empirical counterpart of the choice probability in equation (13). The numerator qjtq_{jt}qjt​ is the number of households that install a system of capacity class jjj in month ttt, observed from the registry of installations. The denominator NtN_tNt​ is the number of households still at risk of adopting at the start of month ttt, defined in equation (15). The ratio is therefore a conditional adoption probability, a discrete-time hazard rate into alternative jjj, and not a share of the installed base or of total sales. Dividing by the remaining population rather than by sales is what makes the outside option, waiting, part of the choice set, so that the level of adoption and not only the mix of capacities is explained.

Equating the observed ratio to the model probability treats NtN_tNt​ as large enough that sampling error in shares is negligible, which is reasonable for the aggregate market and is the reason the approach breaks down for small local markets with many zero shares (see the discussion after equation (26)). In practice monthly adoption shares are very small numbers, so that S0tS_{0t}S0t​ is close to one and

ln⁡(SjtS0t)≈ln⁡Sjt=ln⁡qjt−ln⁡Nt.\ln\left(\frac{S_{jt}}{S_{0t}}\right)\approx\ln S_{jt}=\ln q_{jt}-\ln N_t .ln(S0t​Sjt​​)≈lnSjt​=lnqjt​−lnNt​.

The left-hand side of the estimating equation (18) is thus driven almost entirely by the log number of new installations, and mismeasurement of the potential market mainly shifts the constant.

This defines the potential market in month ttt. The constant NNN is the total number of households that could in principle install a PV system, and the double sum is the cumulative number of adoptions of any capacity in all months before ttt. Because adoption is a terminating action, every adopter leaves the market for good, so the pool of potential adopters shrinks over time. Equivalently, in recursive form,

Nt+1=Nt−∑j=1Jqjt,N1=N.N_{t+1}=N_t-\sum_{j=1}^{J}q_{jt}, \qquad N_{1}=N .Nt+1​=Nt​−j=1∑J​qjt​,N1​=N.

The definition encodes several assumptions: each household adopts at most one system, there is no replacement or upgrading within the sample, and there is no entry of new households or exit of old ones, so NNN is fixed. The sum uses the strict inequality τ<t\tau<tτ<t because adopters in month ttt are still part of the population making a choice in ttt.

The shrinking market matters for interpretation: with a constant adoption probability the number of new installations would fall mechanically over time, so sales qjtq_{jt}qjt​ and shares SjtS_{jt}Sjt​ in equation (14) can move differently. In the application cumulative adoption stays far below NNN, so NtN_tNt​ changes slowly and the correction is modest. In the baseline model with homogeneous households the remaining population has the same preferences as the initial one, so no adjustment for selection is needed; with the local market heterogeneity of equation (25) the same accounting is applied market by market.

The non-adoption share is what is left after all adoption alternatives, since each remaining household chooses exactly one of the J+1J+1J+1 alternatives. From the logit probabilities in equation (13),

∑j=0JSjt=∑j=0Jexp⁡(δjt)∑j′=0Jexp⁡(δj′t)=1⟹S0t=1−∑j=1JSjt.\sum_{j=0}^{J}S_{jt}=\frac{\sum_{j=0}^{J}\exp(\delta_{jt})}{\sum_{j'=0}^{J}\exp(\delta_{j't})}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad S_{0t}=1-\sum_{j=1}^{J}S_{jt}.j=0∑J​Sjt​=∑j′=0J​exp(δj′t​)∑j=0J​exp(δjt​)​=1⟹S0t​=1−j=1∑J​Sjt​.

In terms of the data, insert the definition of the adoption share from equation (14) and then the recursive form of equation (15):

S0t=1−∑j=1JqjtNt=Nt−∑j=1JqjtNt=Nt+1Nt.S_{0t}=1-\sum_{j=1}^{J}\frac{q_{jt}}{N_t}=\frac{N_t-\sum_{j=1}^{J}q_{jt}}{N_t}=\frac{N_{t+1}}{N_t}.S0t​=1−j=1∑J​Nt​qjt​​=Nt​Nt​−∑j=1J​qjt​​=Nt​Nt+1​​.

So S0tS_{0t}S0t​ is the monthly survival rate of the pool of potential adopters: the fraction of households still without a system at the start of month ttt that are still without one at the start of month t+1t+1t+1. It is the model's probability of choosing j=0j=0j=0, that is of the event δ0t+ϵi0t≥max⁡j≥1(δjt+ϵijt)\delta_{0t}+\epsilon_{i0t}\ge\max_{j\ge 1}\left(\delta_{jt}+\epsilon_{ijt}\right)δ0t​+ϵi0t​≥maxj≥1​(δjt​+ϵijt​).

Write the logit share of equation (13) for an adoption alternative jjj and for the waiting alternative; both have the same denominator Dt=∑j′=0Jexp⁡(δj′t)D_t=\sum_{j'=0}^{J}\exp(\delta_{j't})Dt​=∑j′=0J​exp(δj′t​):

Sjt=exp⁡(δjt)Dt,S0t=exp⁡(δ0t)Dt.S_{jt}=\frac{\exp(\delta_{jt})}{D_t}, \qquad S_{0t}=\frac{\exp(\delta_{0t})}{D_t}.Sjt​=Dt​exp(δjt​)​,S0t​=Dt​exp(δ0t​)​.

Dividing, the denominator cancels:

SjtS0t=exp⁡(δjt−δ0t).\frac{S_{jt}}{S_{0t}}=\exp\left(\delta_{jt}-\delta_{0t}\right).S0t​Sjt​​=exp(δjt​−δ0t​).

Taking logs,

ln⁡(SjtS0t)=δjt−δ0t.\ln\left(\frac{S_{jt}}{S_{0t}}\right)=\delta_{jt}-\delta_{0t}.ln(S0t​Sjt​​)=δjt​−δ0t​.

This is the logit share inversion: the observed log odds of adopting jjj relative to waiting reveal the difference in mean values exactly, with no simulation. The difference from the static case is that δ0t\delta_{0t}δ0t​ cannot be normalized to zero. It is the value of waiting, it moves over time with expectations about future prices and subsidies, and it is common to all jjj in month ttt. Equation (12) supplies an expression for it.

Start from the share inversion in equation (17) and substitute the value of waiting from equation (12):

The structure of this error dictates the estimation strategy. The part −β(ξ1,t+1−ηt)-\beta(\xi_{1,t+1}-\eta_t)−β(ξ1,t+1​−ηt​) is common to all jjj within a month, so errors are correlated across alternatives in the same month, and the presence of both ξjt\xi_{jt}ξjt​ and ξ1,t+1\xi_{1,t+1}ξ1,t+1​ induces serial correlation. This is the population orthogonality condition that identifies the parameters of equation (18): the instrument vector zjtz_{jt}zjt​ is uncorrelated with the composite error of equation (19). Using that definition, the condition is the sum of three requirements,

The first two are exclusion restrictions: the instruments must be unrelated to the current demand shock and to next month's demand shock of the reference alternative. The second is an assumption in its own right and is not implied by the first; it holds for instance if zjtz_{jt}zjt​ is exogenous with respect to demand shocks at all dates.

Instruments are needed for the gross price inside pjt(β)p_{jt}(\beta)pjt​(β), which installers may raise when ξjt\xi_{jt}ξjt​ is high, and for the dated t+1t+1t+1 variables p1,t+1(β)p_{1,t+1}(\beta)p1,t+1​(β) and ln⁡S1,t+1\ln S_{1,t+1}lnS1,t+1​. The excluded instruments are cost shifters, chiefly the price index of Chinese PV modules, together with the exogenous components of the net price: the GCC subsidy levels and durations and the other policy variables, which are set by regulation and announced in advance, and the exogenous characteristics xjtx_{jt}xjt​. The module price moves installation costs and so identifies α\alphaα. Variation in future GCC benefits relative to upfront costs, across capacities and over time, identifies β\betaβ through ρtG(β)\rho_t^G(\beta)ρtG​(β), and announced subsidy cuts identify it a second time through the weight on the t+1t+1t+1 terms. Any variable realized only in t+1t+1t+1 is not a valid instrument because it is correlated with ηt\eta_tηt​.

This collects the structural parameters to be estimated from equation (18). The scalar α\alphaα is the marginal utility of money from equation (2). The scalar β\betaβ is the monthly discount factor, which is the object of interest of the paper: it governs both how future subsidies are capitalized (equations (3) to (6)) and how the option of adopting later is valued (equation (7)). The vector γ\gammaγ contains the coefficients on the characteristics xjtx_{jt}xjt​, such as the constant and capacity-size effects.

Estimating β\betaβ is unusual. In most dynamic discrete choice applications the discount factor is fixed at a conventional value because it is poorly identified from choices alone. Here identification is possible because the data contain large policy-driven shifts in future benefits that are distinct from shifts in upfront costs. Everything else in the model is either calibrated from outside information (λ\lambdaλ, π\piπ, ϑ\varthetaϑ, RtGR_t^GRtG​, RER^ERE and the market size NNN) or normalized (u0tu_{0t}u0t​).

The parameters enter very differently. For a given β\betaβ the residual

is linear in (α,γ)(\alpha,\gamma)(α,γ), so these can be concentrated out by linear instrumental variables and the numerical search is effectively over the single nonlinear parameter β\betaβ. In the extension of equation (25) the vector θ\thetaθ is augmented by the interaction coefficients Λ\LambdaΛ.

This is the sample analogue of the population moment condition in equation (20). For a candidate θ\thetaθ the residual ejt(θ)e_{jt}(\theta)ejt​(θ) is computed from data by rearranging equation (18), as written out under equation (21): the observed log odds minus the model's prediction. Each residual is multiplied by the instrument vector zjtz_{jt}zjt​ and the products are averaged over all alternative-month observations. If zjtz_{jt}zjt​ has LLL elements, g(θ)g(\theta)g(θ) is an L×1L\times 1L×1 vector, and identification requires LLL to be at least the number of parameters in θ\thetaθ.

At the true parameter value the law of large numbers gives

while at other values the residual contains a misspecification term correlated with the instruments, so the average stays away from zero. Three practical points. First, the residual for month ttt needs data from month t+1t+1t+1, so the last sample month cannot be used and the effective number of months is one less than the number observed; the factor 1/(JT)1/(JT)1/(JT) is only a normalization and does not affect the minimizer in equation (23). Second, because ηt\eta_tηt​ is common to all alternatives within a month, the convergence relies on the number of months growing, not on JJJ. Third, the error structure in equation (19) implies correlation of zjtejtz_{jt}e_{jt}zjt​ejt​ within months and across adjacent months, which has to be respected when computing standard errors and the efficient weighting matrix.

The estimator picks the parameter vector that brings the sample moments of equation (22) as close to zero as possible, with distance measured by the quadratic form in the positive definite weighting matrix WWW. When there are exactly as many moments as parameters the moments can be set to zero and WWW is irrelevant; with more moments than parameters WWW decides how the conflicting moments are traded off. Any positive definite WWW gives a consistent estimator; efficiency requires WWW to be the inverse of the variance of the moments. The first-order condition is

G(θ^)′ W g(θ^)=0,G(θ)=∂g(θ)∂θ′,G(\hat{\theta})'\,W\,g(\hat{\theta})=0, \qquad G(\theta)=\frac{\partial g(\theta)}{\partial\theta'} ,G(θ^)′Wg(θ^)=0,G(θ)=∂θ′∂g(θ)​,

so the estimator sets a parameter-many set of linear combinations of the moments to zero.

A natural first step uses W=(Z′Z)−1W=(Z'Z)^{-1}W=(Z′Z)−1, where ZZZ stacks the instruments. For fixed β\betaβ the residual is linear in (α,γ)(\alpha,\gamma)(α,γ), so this step is two-stage least squares of the quasi-differenced dependent variable ln⁡(Sjt/S0t)−βln⁡S1,t+1\ln(S_{jt}/S_{0t})-\beta\ln S_{1,t+1}ln(Sjt​/S0t​)−βlnS1,t+1​ on the quasi-differenced regressors, and β\betaβ is found by a one-dimensional search over the concentrated objective. The authors then improve efficiency with an approximation to optimal instruments, which are the conditional expectations of the derivatives of the residual with respect to the parameters, evaluated at the first-step estimate:

This matters most for β\betaβ, whose derivative is a highly nonlinear function of the subsidy variables that simple instruments capture poorly.

The estimated β\betaβ is a discount factor per month. Define the monthly implicit interest rate rmr_mrm​ as the rate that makes a household indifferent between one unit today and 1+rm1+r_m1+rm​ units next month:

1=β (1+rm)⟹1+rm=β−1.1=\beta\,(1+r_m) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 1+r_m=\beta^{-1}.1=β(1+rm​)⟹1+rm​=β−1.

Compounding over the twelve months of a year, one unit today is equivalent to (1+rm)12(1+r_m)^{12}(1+rm​)12 units a year from now. The annual rate rrr is defined by 1+r=(1+rm)121+r=(1+r_m)^{12}1+r=(1+rm​)12, hence

1+r=(β−1)12=β−12⟹r=β−12−1.1+r=\left(\beta^{-1}\right)^{12}=\beta^{-12} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=\beta^{-12}-1 .1+r=(β−1)12=β−12⟹r=β−12−1.

Equivalently the annual discount factor is β12=1/(1+r)\beta^{12}=1/(1+r)β12=1/(1+r), which is the factor already used for the tax credits in equation (6). Since all money amounts in pjt(β)p_{jt}(\beta)pjt​(β) are in real terms, with inflation handled separately in equation (5), rrr is a real interest rate. As a numerical check, a monthly discount factor of β=0.9884\beta=0.9884β=0.9884 gives

r=0.9884−12−1=exp⁡(−12ln⁡0.9884)−1≈e0.140−1≈0.15,r=0.9884^{-12}-1=\exp\left(-12\ln 0.9884\right)-1\approx e^{0.140}-1\approx 0.15,r=0.9884−12−1=exp(−12ln0.9884)−1≈e0.140−1≈0.15,

an implicit real interest rate of about 15 percent per year, the order of magnitude the paper reports and far above market interest rates. Small differences in the monthly factor matter: β=0.9975\beta=0.9975β=0.9975 corresponds to roughly 3 percent per year. This undervaluation of future benefits is why the paper concludes that an upfront investment subsidy would have achieved the same adoption at much lower budgetary cost than the GCC production subsidies.

This extends the mean utility of equation (2) to households living in local market mmm, with m=1,…,Mm=1,\ldots,Mm=1,…,M. The first three terms are the common part δjt\delta_{jt}δjt​, identical across markets and containing the same γ\gammaγ, α\alphaα and demand shock ξjt\xi_{jt}ξjt​ as before; here pjtp_{jt}pjt​ is shorthand for pjt(β)p_{jt}(\beta)pjt​(β). The new term wjtλmw_{jt}\lambda_mwjt​λm​ is a market-specific deviation: wjtw_{jt}wjt​ is a row vector of alternative characteristics that are allowed to be valued differently across markets, typically a constant for adoption, the net price and capacity size, and λm\lambda_mλm​ is the corresponding column vector of market-specific coefficients, defined in equation (26). The symbol λm\lambda_mλm​ here is unrelated to the depreciation rate λ\lambdaλ of equation (5). If the price is an element of wjtw_{jt}wjt​, the price sensitivity in market mmm is α\alphaα minus the corresponding element of λm\lambda_mλm​.

The purpose is to relax the homogeneity of the baseline. Heterogeneity that is persistent over time creates dynamic selection: markets with a high taste for PV adopt early, so the remaining population becomes less eager, and ignoring this could bias the estimated discount factor. Tracking the remaining population NmtN_{mt}Nmt​ market by market handles this. The dynamic structure carries over within each market, with market-specific shares:

ln⁡(SmjtSm0t)=vmjt−β(vm1,t+1−ln⁡Sm1,t+1−ηt).\ln\left(\frac{S_{mjt}}{S_{m0t}}\right)=v_{mjt}-\beta\left(v_{m1,t+1}-\ln S_{m1,t+1}-\eta_t\right).ln(Sm0t​Smjt​​)=vmjt​−β(vm1,t+1​−lnSm1,t+1​−ηt​).

Because local shares are often zero this relation is not inverted market by market; it defines the local choice probabilities used in the likelihood-based micro-moments, with Sm1,t+1S_{m1,t+1}Sm1,t+1​ predicted in a first stage.

This restricts the market-specific coefficients of equation (25) to be a linear function of observed market characteristics. The vector DmD_mDm​ contains demographics of local market mmm, such as income, household size and house size, together with local-market fixed effects, and Λ\LambdaΛ is a matrix of parameters with one row per element of wjtw_{jt}wjt​ and one column per element of DmD_mDm​. Substituting into equation (25) gives

vmjt=δjt+wjtΛDm=δjt+∑k∑lΛkl wjt,k Dm,l,v_{mjt}=\delta_{jt}+w_{jt}\Lambda D_m=\delta_{jt}+\sum_{k}\sum_{l}\Lambda_{kl}\,w_{jt,k}\,D_{m,l},vmjt​=δjt​+wjt​ΛDm​=δjt​+k∑​l∑​Λkl​wjt,k​Dm,l​,

so heterogeneity enters only through interactions between alternative characteristics and market characteristics. Each Λkl\Lambda_{kl}Λkl​ says how the valuation of characteristic kkk shifts with demographic lll: for instance whether higher-income areas are less price sensitive, or whether areas with larger houses prefer larger systems.

The specification is the observed-heterogeneity analogue of random coefficients. There is no unobserved random component in λm\lambda_mλm​, so all households within a market are still identical up to ϵijt\epsilon_{ijt}ϵijt​, and no simulation over unobserved types is needed. The interaction coefficients Λ\LambdaΛ are identified from cross-market variation: the covariance between market demographics and the characteristics of the systems adopted there, and differences in total adoption rates across markets. These are exactly the micro-moments that are added to the aggregate moments of equation (20), while α\alphaα, β\betaβ and γ\gammaγ remain identified by the time-series and cross-capacity variation in the aggregate equation (18). Setting Λ=0\Lambda=0Λ=0 returns the baseline model.
